sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Randolph County, NC?
sections.html:
The Randolph County Tax Department handles listing, appraisal and bills for the county. Its website carries pages for real property, tax rates, reappraisal, tax liens, the annual tax scroll, property tax relief and foreclosure sales.

Randolph is made up of several towns, and the rate page lists city rates for Asheboro, Archdale, Franklinville, Liberty, Ramseur, Randleman, Seagrove, Staley, High Point, Thomasville and Trinity. Which charges land on your bill depends on whether your parcel is inside one of those municipalities or a fire district.

sections.h2: What rates does Randolph County list for 2026-2027?
sections.html:
The county's tax rate page, headed 2026-2027, lists a county rate of 0.50. Confirm the rate on your own bill with the tax department, because this page does not say the word adopted.

The same page lists separate city, school and fire rates, which is where most of the difference between addresses comes from. A few of the figures it prints:

  • City rates: Asheboro 0.71, Archdale 0.31, Liberty 0.72, Randleman 0.63, Thomasville 0.62, High Point 0.7349, Trinity 0.10.
  • School rates: Asheboro 0.1153 and Trinity 0.0803.
  • Fire rates run from 0.10 for Staley to 0.18 for Climax.
  • Vehicle fees are listed for High Point (30.00 flat), Liberty (5.00 flat) and Thomasville (20.00 flat).

sections.h2: How often does Randolph County revalue property?
sections.html:
Every four years. The state minimum is eight, and the county's real property page says Randolph chose a shorter cycle. The last reappraisal took effect January 1, 2023, and the next is scheduled for 2027.

The county has posted a proposed 2027 schedule of values and a proposed present use value schedule, so those are drafts until the commissioners act. Under G.S. 105-286, counties may set a more frequent cycle by resolution. A revaluation year is when many sellers see the biggest shift in assessed value, so it pays to read the notice carefully.

sections.h2: How does Randolph County set the value of a house?
sections.html:
The county's reappraisal page says appraisers study sales data from real estate transactions in the county, record each property's size, construction type, heating and cooling, plumbing, age and condition, and also consider the income a property could produce.

The stated goal is to appraise real estate at 100 percent of market value. The page also says property values do not move uniformly across the county: depending on recent sales in a market area, an assessment may rise, fall or stay about the same. The state's definition is the price at which property would change hands between a willing buyer and willing seller, neither under compulsion.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Randolph County assessment?
sections.html:
The county lists four steps: an informal appeal, the Randolph County Board of Equalization and Review, the North Carolina Property Tax Commission, and the appellate court. Informal appeal forms are mailed with each reappraisal value notice.

Randolph's page names two valid reasons: the assessment substantially exceeds market value, or it is inconsistent with similar properties in your market area. It lists as invalid reasons that the value is just too high, that the taxes are too high, or that the owner cannot afford the bill. State law adds the timing. The board of equalization and review first meets no earlier than the first Monday in April and no later than the first Monday in May under G.S. 105-322, and a Commission appeal is due within 30 days after the board mails its decision under G.S. 105-290.

sections.h2: Who is billed if a Randolph County house sells?
sections.html:
The January 1 owner. The county's real property page says the tax bill is always generated for the owner as of January 1, and that a permanent listing system lists real property automatically once a deed is recorded with the Register of Deeds. Changes to buildings must be reported during the listing period.

State law, G.S. 105-360, makes taxes due September 1, payable at face value through January 5, with 2 percent interest from January 6 and three-fourths of one percent a month from February 1. The tax also becomes a lien under G.S. 105-355 as of the listing date. In a sale, the closing attorney settles who pays the year's bill.

sections.h2: What is the circuit breaker deferment in North Carolina?
sections.html:
It caps the tax for qualifying older or disabled owners. Under G.S. 105-277.1B, tax is limited to 4.0 percent of income if income is at or below the eligibility limit and 5.0 percent if income is above it up to 150 percent of the limit. The owner must be 65 or older, or totally and permanently disabled, and must have lived in the home as a permanent residence for five years.

The excess is deferred, and it is a lien. Deferred taxes for the three preceding fiscal years come due if the home is transferred, the owner dies or the owner stops living there. A sale triggers repayment at closing. An owner can apply only for one of the three relief programs, so ask the Randolph County tax department which one fits.

sections.h2: When can Randolph County owners list property and report changes?
sections.html:
The state listing period begins the first business day of January and ends January 31 under G.S. 105-307. Commissioners may extend it by up to 30 days in a nonrevaluation year and 60 days in a revaluation year, and individual owners can ask for a good-cause extension, though not past April 15.

In Randolph the listing of land is automatic once a deed is recorded, so the listing period matters mostly for building changes and for personal property such as business equipment. If you added a room or removed a structure, tell the tax department during that window, since the bill follows what is on the record.

sections.h2: What relief or collection rules matter to a Randolph County seller?
sections.html:
The elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or half the home's appraised value under G.S. 105-277.1, and the disabled veteran exclusion removes the first $45,000 under G.S. 105-277.1C. The county's tax relief page is where to apply. Ask the tax department about the filing window.

If taxes stay unpaid, the county can foreclose, and a tax sale is a public auction at the courthouse door under G.S. 105-374. A person redeeming before confirmation pays all taxes plus penalties, interest and costs. Selling first and paying the bill from proceeds avoids that path. A cash buyer can often close fast enough to do it.

faqs.q: What is Randolph County's reappraisal schedule?
faqs.a: Every four years. The last reappraisal took effect January 1, 2023, and the county says the next one is scheduled for 2027.

faqs.q: What county rate does Randolph County list for 2026-2027?
faqs.a: Its tax rate page lists 0.50 for the county. City, school and fire rates are listed separately, so call the tax department to confirm your total.

faqs.q: Can I appeal because my taxes are too high?
faqs.a: No. Randolph's reappraisal page lists taxes being too high or an owner's inability to pay as invalid reasons. A valid appeal says the value exceeds market value or is out of line with similar properties.

faqs.q: When does interest start on unpaid Randolph County tax?
faqs.a: After January 5. G.S. 105-360 sets 2 percent from January 6 to February 1, then three-fourths of one percent per month.

faqs.q: Who gets the tax bill after I sell my Randolph County house?
faqs.a: The county says the bill is generated for the January 1 owner. Settle any split with the buyer at closing.
